reason: Complete the agreed concise Objective–Methods–Results–Contribution abstract with correct three-model evidence.
before: Road-damage detectors are often evaluated on imagery collected under conditions resembling the training data. Their performance under a change of acquisition domain can be markedly different. \textbf{This study aims to quantify the magnitude and asymmetry of domain shift when deploying road-damage detectors across different camera platforms, and to identify which damage classes are most vulnerable under cross-domain conditions.} We measure bidirectional transfer between the China\_Drone and China\_MotorBike subsets of RDD2022, using a scene-aware split and a comparison that holds the target test set fixed. The locked subset contains 4,378 images and four damage classes. We fine-tune COCO-pretrained YOLO11n and YOLOv8n independently on each domain, with three matched random seeds and 150 epochs per run (12 runs in total). On Drone Test, the mean in-domain advantage in bounding-box mAP@50:95 is \textbf{15.13 $\pm$ 3.85 percentage points} for YOLO11n and \textbf{14.86 $\pm$ 1.25} for YOLOv8n. On MotorBike Test, the respective gaps are \textbf{42.94 $\pm$ 0.52} and \textbf{41.24 $\pm$ 1.04}. Values denote mean $\pm$ sample standard deviation over three seeds. All fixed-target gaps are positive, yet their magnitude is asymmetric and class dependent. \textbf{Aggregating across architectures and directions, the mean relative performance drop from in-domain to out-of-domain deployment is 54.67\%, with D20 (alligator cracks) experiencing a 94.3\% decline and D00 (longitudinal cracks) showing 35.3\% degradation.} The findings describe a substantial domain-associated performance gap under this benchmark; differences in camera geometry, collection conditions, source sample sizes, and class distributions are not experimentally disentangled. The study contributes a reproducible evaluation protocol and a two-architecture replication rather than a new detector.
after: Road-damage detectors are often evaluated on imagery resembling their training data, yet deployment across camera platforms can reduce accuracy. This study quantifies the magnitude, asymmetry, and class dependence of cross-domain transfer between the China\_Drone and China\_MotorBike subsets of RDD2022. We use a scene-aware split and compare target-domain-trained and other-domain-trained detectors on identical held-out target images. The locked subset contains 4,378 images, including 658 test images, and four damage classes. COCO-pretrained YOLO11n, YOLOv8n, and YOLO26n are independently fine-tuned on each domain with three matched seeds and 150 epochs per run (18 runs). Mean fixed-target mAP@50:95 gaps range from 14.86 to 16.91 percentage points on Drone Test and from 41.24 to 42.94 points on MotorBike Test. For YOLO26n, the respective gaps are $16.91\pm0.80$ and $42.27\pm1.28$ points, where uncertainty is sample standard deviation over three seeds. All 18 seed-specific comparisons favor target-domain training. On MotorBike Test, D20 relative class-AP declines range from 96.14\% to 98.30\% against the target-trained baselines. YOLO26n improves mean in-domain mAP over YOLOv8n by 3.08 and 3.50 points on Drone and MotorBike, respectively, while substantial gaps persist. The study contributes a reproducible bidirectional protocol and a three-variant replication of domain-associated asymmetry and class-specific vulnerability. Acquisition geometry, training size, and other collection differences remain jointly varying factors.

before: \textbf{Consensus: domain shift degrades detection.} Multiple studies agree that object detectors trained on one visual distribution suffer performance loss when deployed under different acquisition conditions. The domain-generalization literature cautions that success on source-like data may not carry to a shifted target distribution \cite{zhou2023survey}; large benchmarks such as WILDS \cite{koh2021wilds} and COCO \cite{lin2014coco} illustrate that preserving meaningful dataset boundaries is essential for valid performance claims. Road-damage detection follows this pattern: Maeda \emph{et al.} \cite{maeda2018road} introduced smartphone-image classification, and Arya \emph{et al.} \cite{arya2024rdd2022} documented the multinational RDD2022 dataset's acquisition diversity, implicitly acknowledging that camera platform matters.

before: \textbf{Trade-off: adaptation vs. controlled measurement.} One line of work develops architectures or adaptation strategies to improve cross-domain robustness. For example, YOLO-RD \cite{wang2025yolord} proposes detector enhancements for pavement distress. Such enhancement-oriented studies typically evaluate on a particular subset with architecture-specific tuning, making direct numerical comparison across papers difficult when dataset partitions, model sizes, label filtering, and validation protocols are not aligned. An alternative approach—adopted here—holds the detector and training protocol fixed while systematically varying only the source acquisition domain, trading adaptation gains for clearer causal attribution of performance differences to domain choice.

\textbf{Trade-off: adaptation vs. controlled measurement.} One line of work develops architectures or adaptation strategies to improve cross-domain robustness. For example, YOLO-RD \cite{wang2025yolord} proposes detector enhancements for pavement distress. Such enhancement-oriented studies typically evaluate on a particular subset with architecture-specific tuning, making direct numerical comparison across papers difficult when dataset partitions, model sizes, label filtering, and validation protocols are not aligned. An alternative approach—adopted here—holds each detector's explicit fine-tuning settings fixed while varying the source acquisition domain, prioritizing a clear measurement of domain-associated performance differences.

\textbf{YOLO family evolution.} YOLOv8 \cite{ultralyticsyolov8}, YOLO11 \cite{jocher2024yolo11}, and YOLO26 \cite{ultralyticsyolo26} provide related compact detector variants with different pretrained checkpoints and model-specific implementations. Repeating the same fixed-target protocol across them tests whether the observed gap is confined to one variant. Matched explicit fine-tuning settings improve comparability, while architecture, pretraining, and implementation differences remain coupled.

before: \textbf{Gap: bidirectional asymmetry and class-level vulnerability remain unmeasured.} Existing work often compares one model on two different test sets, conflating model transfer with intrinsic test-set difficulty. No prior study on RDD2022 has quantified \emph{bidirectional} transfer gaps using a fixed target, nor isolated which damage classes (D00, D10, D20, D40) are most vulnerable when acquisition geometry shifts. WILDS-style evaluations emphasize distribution shifts but rarely focus on road infrastructure, and architecture papers prioritize overall mAP without per-class fragility analysis.
after: \textbf{Gap: bidirectional asymmetry and class-level vulnerability.} Comparing one model on two different test sets conflates transfer behavior with intrinsic test-set difficulty. A fixed-target comparison is needed to quantify the advantage of target-domain training on each acquisition domain and to determine how that contrast varies across D00, D10, D20, and D40. The question addressed here is how large these two target-specific gaps are, whether their direction recurs across seeds and models, and which classes depart from the aggregate pattern.

after: \textbf{Comparison with prior work.} Our findings support the motivation for distribution-aware evaluation in domain-generalization research and WILDS \cite{zhou2023survey,koh2021wilds}, while focusing on two road-acquisition domains and their class-specific contrasts. COCO \cite{lin2014coco} supplies the pretraining context rather than evidence of adaptation on these road datasets. The MotorBike-target advantage exceeds the Drone-target advantage by 27.80, 26.38, and 25.36~pp for YOLO11n, YOLOv8n, and YOLO26n, respectively.
